claim_records.text: The proposed method shows a significant improvement in accuracy in the miniImageNet benchmark compared to other metric-based few-shot learning methods by a margin of 2%.
The proposed method demonstrates competitive generalization capabilities to other domains, such as the Caltech CUB, Dogs and Cars datasets compared with the state of the art.
The ICNN loss is based on an inter and intra class nearest neighbors score, which helps assess the quality of embeddings obtained from the trained network.
The Proto-Triplet Loss is based on the original triplet loss with modifications needed to better work on few-shot scenarios.
The ICNN loss represents a novel loss function that evaluates the quality of features obtained based on inter/intra class, variance and class ratio from nearest neighbors.
Using the proto-triplet loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 61.32% in the 5-way 1-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
Using the proto-triplet loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 79.93% in the 5-way 5-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
Using the ICNN Loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 60.79% in the 5-way 1-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
Using the ICNN Loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 80.41% in the 5-way 5-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
The obtained accuracy performance on Mini-Imagenet represents an improvement of about 2% compared to the state of the art.
The methods are further tested on the CUB, Caltech, Stanford Dogs and Stanford Cars datasets to assess generalization capabilities, obtaining satisfactory results.

claim_records.text: The introduced flexible architecture, where class representations are conditioned for each few-shot trial based on a target image and comparisons between classes are performed by a trained network rather than relying on static metric comparison, achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Caltech-UCSD birds fine-grained classification task.

The proposed few-shot architecture replaces metric space comparison with a learned neural network, producing a softmax probability distribution rather than a true distance or similarity metric, so it is not a true metric-learning approach.
The network achieves its best performance only when it is allowed to condition each class representation based on the target, or query, image.
The network consists of four distinct stages trained fully end-to-end: a feature stage, a relational stage, a conditioning stage, and a classifier.

The feature stage uses a convolutional architecture with four convolutional blocks, each containing a 2D convolutional layer with 3×3 kernel and 32 filters, followed by batch normalization, ELU activation, and 2×2 max pooling, with a final linear layer producing an 800-dimensional image representation.
The relational stage compares images within a class in a pairwise fashion using shared parameters across all classes, producing a single vector to represent the class.
The conditioning stage uses the query image to augment the representation for each class.
The classifier stage combines information across class vectors and produces a final softmax classification based on the query image.
Relational networks for few-shot class representation are order-insensitive, allowing treatment of support set images for a single class as an unordered input set.

claim_records.text: The proposed hybrid Meta-Metric-Learner combines optimization-based and metric-based meta-learning, consisting of a task-specific metric-based learner as a base model and a meta-learner that learns and specifies the base model.
The Meta-Metric-Learner is able to handle flexible numbers of classes as well as generate more generalized metrics for classification across tasks.

Optimization-based meta-learning approaches require task-specific classifiers to be homogeneous-structured to ease parameter prediction, so they can only handle few-shot learning problems where tasks share a uniform number of classes.
Metric-based meta-learning approaches learn one task-invariant metric for all tasks, and require tasks to come from a similar domain such that a uniform metric works across tasks.

Experiments show the Meta-Metric-Learner approach obtains superior performance in both the standard k-shot N-way few-shot setting and the new realistic few-shot setting with flexible class numbers in single-source and multi-source forms.

The meta learner operating across tasks uses an optimization-based meta-model to discover good parameters and gradient descent in task-specific base learners, while the base learner exploits a metric-based model parameterized by weight prediction from the optimization-based meta-learner.
The proposed model is able to handle unbalanced classes in meta-train and meta-test sets and generate task-specific metrics leveraging weight prediction of the meta-learner given task instances.
Existing optimization-based few-shot learning approaches cannot resolve the issue of heterogeneous-structured task-specific networks arising when tasks have different numbers of labels.
The learned task-invariant metric of metric-based approaches may not generalize well if tasks diverge, and no uniform metric is suitable for all tasks from different domains or data sources.

claim_records.text: The proposed adaptive metric learning approach automatically determines the best weighted combination from a set of metrics obtained from meta-training tasks for a newly seen few-shot task.

Extensive quantitative evaluations on real-world sentiment analysis and dialog intent classification datasets demonstrate that the proposed method performs favorably against state-of-the-art few shot learning algorithms in terms of predictive accuracy.

The proposed task-clustering framework for diverse few-shot learning starts with a novel task clustering algorithm based on matrix completion, followed by a few-shot learning method based on task clustering.

fact_fields.method: task-clustering framework with matrix completion-based task clustering

claim_records.text: Directly using transfer performance for task clustering requires conducting source-target transfer learning O(n^2) times, where n is the number of meta-training tasks.
For a large number of diverse tasks where n can be larger than 1,000, evaluation of the full transfer performance matrix is unacceptable because it requires over 1M entries to evaluate.
The proposed matrix completion-based task clustering algorithm deals with the huge number of transfer performance entries by randomly sampling task pairs to evaluate S_ij and S_ji scores.
The proposed matrix completion-based task clustering algorithm deals with unreliable entries and asymmetry issue by keeping only task pairs (i, j) with consistent S_ij and S_ji scores.
Few-shot learning aims to learn classifiers from few examples per class.
Deep learning-based FSL learns meta-models from a large number of meta-training tasks, which can then be used for rapid adaptation for target/meta-testing tasks that only have few training examples.

Previous FSL works mainly considered image domains such as Omniglot and ImageNet, where tasks are sampled from a single domain and thus related, leading to almost all previous works employing a common meta-model for all few-shot tasks.
In enterprise AI cloud service scenarios, submitted text classification tasks are significantly diverse, thus a common metric is insufficient to handle all these tasks.

claim_records.text: Deep metric learning methods for few-shot image classification classify unseen samples according to their distances to few seen samples in an embedding space learned by powerful deep neural networks, avoiding overfitting to few training images.

This review categorizes deep metric learning methods for few-shot image classification from 2018 to 2022 into three groups according to three stages of metric learning: learning feature embeddings, learning class representations, and learning distance measures.

In few-shot classification, the metric is learned on the base dataset; query images of the novel class are classified by computing their distances to novel support images with respect to the learned measure, followed by applying a distance-based classifier such as k-nearest.

fact_fields.method: supervised metric learning for few-shot classification

claim_records.text: Early few-shot metric learning methods such as Siamese Network and Matching Network classify a query sample by measuring and comparing its distance to support samples.
Class prototypes can be constructed by taking simple or weighted average of feature embeddings, or learned in an end-to-end manner to improve their representation ability.

Zhang et al. proposed a variational Bayesian framework for few-shot learning that uses the Kullback-Leibler divergence to measure the distance of samples, and can compute the confidence that a query image is assigned into each class by estimating the distribution of each class based on a neural network.

fact_fields.method: variational Bayesian framework for few-shot learning

claim_records.text: Simon et al. proposed Deep Subspace Network (DSN) to represent each class using a low-dimensional subspace constructed from support samples via singular value decomposition.

DSN classifies query samples according to the nearest subspace classifier, assigning the query to the class which has the shortest Euclidean distance between the query and its projection onto the class-specific subspace.
DSN is shown to be more robust to noises and outliers than Prototoypical Network.
Few-shot classification is defined as learning a classification rule from few (typically 1-5) labeled examples.
The biggest challenge in few-shot classification is a high risk of model overfitting to the few labeled training samples.
Meta-learning methods train a meta-learner on many different classification tasks to extract generalizable knowledge, which enables rapid learning on a new related task with few examples.
Transfer learning methods presume shared knowledge between the source and target domains, and fine-tune the model trained on abundant source data to fit few labeled target samples.

Metric learning methods learn feature embeddings and/or distance measures and classify an unseen sample based on its distance to labeled samples or class representations; samples of the same class are expected to locate close together in the embedding space and samples of different classes should be far apart.

claim_records.text: The Uncertainty-Aware Few-Shot (UAFS) framework models uncertainty of query-prototype similarity and performs uncertainty-aware optimization for few-shot image classification.

For a query sample and N prototypes in the support set, each query-prototype pair is treated as a node and a graph-based model is employed to jointly infer the similarity uncertainty for each query-prototype pair.

The similarity between a query feature and a prototype feature is modeled by a distribution (probabilistic similarity) based on graph-based similarity uncertainty estimation, rather than a scalar, to alleviate the influence of observation noises.

fact_fields.method: probabilistic similarity modeling based on graph-based similarity uncertainty estimation

claim_records.text: The network is optimized with similarity-based classification losses which exploit the estimated uncertainty.

fact_fields.method: similarity-based classification losses exploiting estimated uncertainty

claim_records.text: The proposed Uncertainty-Aware Few-Shot framework converts observed similarities to probabilistic representations and incorporates them to the loss for more effective optimization.
A graph-based model is utilized to estimate the uncertainty of query-support pairs in order to jointly consider the similarities between a query and the prototypes in a support set.
Extensive experiments show the proposed method brings significant improvements on top of a strong baseline and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

Good feature embedding is important to deliver favorable performance for similarity-based few-shot image classification, and the set of category-specific prototypes plays the role of a similarity-based classifier to identify the category of a query sample by finding the nearest prototype over the support set in the embedding space.
During training, for a query sample, the logit vector (classification probability) is obtained by feeding the similarities between the query sample and the prototypes to a SoftMax function.

fact_fields.method: SoftMax function applied to query-prototype similarities

claim_records.text: The reliability of the estimated similarity is vital to few-shot image classification performance.
Aleatoric uncertainty identifies the confidence level of the network on its output for a sample, which captures the noise inherent in the observations.

For few-shot image classification, the network has different uncertainties on the calculated similarities of different query-prototype pairs, and an observed similarity of a query-prototype pair, being a one time sampling, suffers from observation noise, where higher uncertainty means less reliable estimated similarity.
For each few-shot task during optimization, the number of experienced query-prototype pairs is limited, and the side effect of observation noises due to high uncertainty limits the optimization.

For each query-prototype pair, the proposed framework converts the observed feature similarity between the query and the prototype from a deterministic scalar to a distribution, with the variance of this distribution characterizing the uncertainty of the observed similarity.

fact_fields.method: conversion of observed feature similarity from scalar to distribution

claim_records.text: The core idea of the proposed method is to use feature-wise transformation layers for augmenting image features using affine transforms to simulate various feature distributions under different domains in the training stage.

fact_fields.method: feature-wise transformation layers with affine transforms

claim_records.text: A learning-to-learn approach is further applied to search for the hyper-parameters of the feature-wise transformation layers to capture variations of the feature distributions under different domains.
Extensive experiments and ablation studies are conducted under the domain generalization setting using five few-shot classification datasets: mini-ImageNet, CUB, Cars, Places, and Plantae.

Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed feature-wise transformation layer is applicable to various metric-based models, and provides consistent improvements on the few-shot classification performance under domain shift.

Metric-based few-shot classification methods consist of a feature encoder and a metric function: given an input task with support set and query set from novel classes, the encoder first extracts image features, and the metric function takes features of both labeled and unlabeled images as input to predict the category of query images.
Existing metric-based approaches often do not generalize well to categories from different domains, despite success recognizing novel classes sampled from the same domain as the training stage.
The key observation is that the distributions of image features extracted from tasks in unseen domains are significantly different from those in seen domains.
Unsupervised domain adaptation approaches assume that numerous unlabeled images are available in the target domain during training, which may not be realistic in many cases.
Existing domain generalization approaches aim at recognizing instances from the same category in the training stage.
During the training stage, the metric function may overfit to the feature distributions encoded only from seen domains and thus fail to generalize to unseen domains.

The proposed feature-wise transformation layers modulate feature activations with affine transformations integrated into the feature encoder, simulating various distributions of image features during training to improve the generalization ability of the metric function in the testing phase.

fact_fields.method: feature-wise transformation layers integrated into feature encoder

claim_records.text: The hyper-parameters of the feature-wise transformation layers may require meticulous hand-tuning due to the difficulty to model the complex variation of image feature distributions across various domains.

A learning-to-learn algorithm is developed to optimize the proposed feature-wise transformation layers, with the core idea to optimize the layers so that the model can work well on unseen domains after training using seen domains.
The proposed feature-wise transformation layers are method-agnostic and can be applied to various metric-based few-shot classification approaches for improving their generalization to unseen domains.

claim_records.text: Region Comparison Network (RCN) is a metric learning based method for few-shot image classification that aims to reveal how few-shot learning works in a neural network and identify specific related regions in query and support images.
Region Activation Mapping (RAM) is a visualization strategy designed to intuitively explain what RCN has learned by visualizing intermediate variables in the network.
Experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of RCN over existing baselines for few-shot image classification.
Few-shot learning aims to learn a classifier for a given set of classes using only limited labeled training samples.
Existing few-shot learning works based on metric learning include matching networks, prototypical networks, and relation networks, while gradient-based methods include MAML and MetaSGD.

fact_fields.method: metric-based and gradient-based few-shot learning models

claim_records.text: RCN's region meta learner is designed as a dynamic system to adapt to different meta tasks during the training and testing stages.

RCN directly indicates the relationship between final classification decisions and region similarities in the last layer, which is a simple and easily explained linear process compared to attention mechanisms.
RCN learns a generated weight of regions to explain which regions in a support sample are similar to regions in a query sample and which regions the model prefers to compare.

claim_records.text: The Relation Network (RN) is trained end-to-end from scratch for few-shot learning.
During meta-learning, the Relation Network learns a deep distance metric to compare small numbers of images within episodes designed to simulate the few-shot setting.
Once trained, a Relation Network classifies images of new classes by computing relation scores between query images and few examples of each new class without further updating the network.
The Relation Network framework is easily extended to zero-shot learning in addition to few-shot learning.
Extensive experiments on five benchmarks demonstrate the Relation Network provides a unified and effective approach for both few-shot and zero-shot learning tasks.

claim_records.text: Existing CLIP-based few-shot classification approaches such as CoOp and Tip-Adapter only focus on high-level visual features fully aligned with textual features representing the summary of an image.
Low-level local representations (LRs) are more consistent between seen and unseen samples than high-level representations for few-shot image classification.
The proposed Meta-Feature Adaption method (MF-Adapter) combines complementary strengths of local representations and high-level semantic representations for few-shot classification.
The Meta-Feature Unit (MF-Unit) is a simple yet effective local similarity metric that measures category-consistent local context in an inductive manner.
The MF-Adapter is trained to map image features to MF-Unit to adequately generalize intra-class knowledge between unseen images and the support set.

Extensive experiments show the proposed MF-Adapter method is superior to state-of-the-art CLIP downstream few-shot classification methods, with stronger performance on a set of challenging visual classification tasks.

claim_records.text: The proposed subspace representation learning (SRL) framework represents an image using a subspace in local CNN feature space and measures similarity between two images via a weighted subspace distance (WSD).
When K images are available per class, the SRL framework develops two types of template subspaces to aggregate K-shot information: the prototypical subspace (PS) and the discriminative subspace (DS).
The SRL framework extends metric learning based techniques from vector to subspace representation.
Using subspace representation can effectively preserve the spatial structure and diversity within an image, in contrast to most previous works that adopted global vector representation.

The SRL framework demonstrates competitive or superior performance compared to previous state-of-the-art methods on the MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet, and Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 (CUB) public benchmark datasets.

claim_records.text: Local descriptor based representations can achieve richer representations than image-level based representations for few-shot learning.
Existing local descriptor based few-shot learning works still rely on a less effective instance-level symmetric metric to measure relations between query images and support classes.
An asymmetric measure is more suitable for metric-based few-shot learning, given the natural asymmetric relation between a query image and a support class.

The proposed Asymmetric Distribution Measure (ADM) network calculates a joint local and global asymmetric measure between two multivariate local distributions of queries and classes for few-shot learning.
A task-aware Contrastive Measure Strategy (CMS) is proposed to further enhance the measure function in the ADM network.
The ADM network achieves a 3.02% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task on miniImageNet.
The ADM network achieves a 1.56% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task on tieredImageNet.

claim_records.text: The RankDNN few-shot learning pipeline casts relevance ranking for image retrieval as binary ranking relation classification.
Compared to image classification, ranking relation classification is sample efficient and domain agnostic.
The core component of RankDNN is a simple MLP that takes an image triplet encoded as the difference between two vector-Kronecker products as input and outputs a binary relevance ranking order.
RankMLP can be built on top of any state-of-the-art feature extractors.
RankDNN can be flexibly fused with other post-processing methods.
During meta test, RankDNN ranks support images according to their similarity with query samples, and each query sample is assigned the class label of its nearest neighbor.
RankDNN can effectively improve the performance of its baselines based on a variety of backbones.
RankDNN outperforms previous state-of-the-art algorithms on multiple few-shot learning benchmarks including miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, Caltech-UCSD Birds, and CIFAR-FS.
Experiments on the cross-domain challenge demonstrate the superior transferability of RankDNN.

claim_records.text: The developed few-shot image classification methods employ the Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) as a metric to compute structural distance between dense image representations to determine image relevance.

fact_fields.method: Few-shot image classification methods using Earth Mover's Distance (EMD)

claim_records.text: The EMD generates optimal matching flows between structural elements that have the minimum matching cost, which is used to calculate the image distance for classification.

A cross-reference mechanism is designed to generate important weights of elements in the EMD formulation, which can effectively alleviate the adverse impact caused by cluttered background and large intra-class appearance variations.
To implement k-shot classification, a structured fully connected layer is proposed that can directly classify dense image representations with the EMD.
Based on the implicit function theorem, the EMD can be inserted as a layer into the network for end-to-end training.

claim_records.text: The proposed algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin on five widely used few-shot classification benchmarks: miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, Fewshot-CIFAR100 (FC100), Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 (CUB), and CIFAR-FewShot (CIFAR-FS).
The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated on the image retrieval task in experiments.

claim_records.text: Traditional metric-based few-shot classification methods typically rely on a single distance value between the query feature and support feature, thereby overlooking the contribution of shallow features.

The proposed approach uses a multi-output embedding network that maps samples into distinct feature spaces, extracting feature vectors at different stages to enable the model to capture both global and abstract features.

claim_records.text: The proposed Siamese Transformer Network (STN) uses two parallel branch networks built on the pre-trained Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture to extract global and local features respectively.
The STN implementation uses the ViT-Small network architecture, with branch networks initialized using pre-trained model parameters obtained through self-supervised learning.
STN applies the Euclidean distance measure to global features and the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence measure to local features.
STN integrates the two feature similarity metrics by first applying L2 normalization, then weighting the normalized results to obtain the final similarity score.
STN adopts a meta-learning approach to fine-tune the entire network during the training phase.
The STN framework achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines on four popular few-shot classification benchmarks in both 5-shot and 1-shot scenarios.

FAFD-LDWR outperforms state-of-the-art methods on three benchmark datasets in both 1-shot and 5-shot settings.
Designed visualization experiments demonstrate that FAFD-LDWR improves prediction interpretability.

Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that MSPL outperforms traditional approaches in detecting low-profile and novel attack types.

claim_records.text: The key issue of few-shot learning is learning to generalize.
This paper proposes a large margin principle to improve the generalization capacity of metric based methods for few-shot learning.
A unified framework is developed to learn a more discriminative metric space by augmenting the classification loss function with a large margin distance loss function for training.

Extensive experiments on graph neural networks and prototypical networks show that the proposed method can improve the performance of existing models substantially with very little computational overhead.

claim_records.text: Learning from a few examples remains a key challenge in machine learning.
The standard supervised deep learning paradigm does not offer a satisfactory solution for learning new concepts rapidly from little data.
The proposed framework learns a network that maps a small labelled support set and an unlabelled example to its label, obviating the need for fine-tuning to adapt to new class types.
The proposed algorithm improves one-shot accuracy on ImageNet from 87.6% to 93.2% compared to competing approaches.
The proposed algorithm improves one-shot accuracy on Omniglot from 88.0% to 93.8% compared to competing approaches.
The same model demonstrates usefulness on language modeling by introducing a one-shot task on the Penn Treebank.

claim_records.text: Mutual Centralized Learning (MCL) associates each local feature with a particle that can bidirectionally random walk in a discrete feature space by the affiliations.
MCL uses the features' accessibility, which measures the expected number of visits to the support features of that class in a Markov process, to estimate class probability.
MCL is related to learning a centrality on an affiliation network and can be plugged in existing methods by highlighting centralized local features.
Experiments show that MCL achieves the state-of-the-art on both miniImageNet and tieredImageNet.

claim_records.text: The proposed LaSO method combines pairs of given examples in feature space, so that the resulting synthesized feature vectors correspond to examples whose label sets are obtained through certain set operations on the label sets of the corresponding input pairs.
The LaSO method is capable of producing a sample containing the intersection, union or set-difference of labels present in two input samples.
The set operations used in LaSO generalize to labels unseen during training, enabling augmentation on examples of novel categories for multi-label few-shot classifier learning.

Experiments show promising results for the label-set manipulation capabilities of the proposed LaSO approach, both directly using classification and retrieval metrics, and in the context of performing data augmentation for multi-label few-shot learning.
The proposed LaSO method compares favorably to all the common baselines on the newly proposed benchmark for multi-label few-shot classification.

claim_records.text: Existing cache-based adaptation approaches such as Tip-Adapter inherit CLIP's tendency to encode global, general-purpose representations that are not optimally discriminative for adapting the generalist to the specialist's domain in low-data regimes.

The proposed relational gated graph attention network constructs a patch graph and performs edge-aware attention to emphasize informative inter-patch interactions, producing context-enriched patch embeddings.
A learnable multi-aggregation pooling composes context-enriched patch embeddings into compact, task-discriminative representations that better align cache keys with the target few-shot classes.
The proposed graph refinement is used only during training to distil relational structure into the cache, incurring no additional inference cost beyond standard cache lookup.
Final predictions are obtained by a residual fusion of cache similarity scores with CLIP zero-shot logits.

claim_records.text: HelixFormer is a Transformer-based double-helix model designed to achieve cross-image object semantic relation mining in a bidirectional and symmetrical manner for few-shot fine-grained image classification.
HelixFormer consists of two sequential steps: 1) Relation Mining Process (RMP) across different branches, and 2) Representation Enhancement Process (REP) within each individual branch.

The designed RMP enables each HelixFormer branch to extract fine-grained object-level Cross-image Semantic Relation Maps (CSRMs) using information from the other branch, to improve cross-image interaction in semantically related local object regions.

With the aid of extracted CSRMs, the developed REP strengthens extracted features for discovered semantically-related local regions in each HelixFormer branch, boosting the model's ability to distinguish subtle fine-grained object feature differences.
Experiments conducted on five public fine-grained benchmarks show HelixFormer achieves better performance over most state-of-the-art methods under both 1-shot and 5-shot few-shot scenarios.
The official code implementation of HelixFormer is publicly available at https://github.com/JiakangYuan/HelixFormer.

claim_records.text: The proposed method shows a significant improvement in accuracy in the miniImageNet benchmark compared to other metric-based few-shot learning methods by a margin of 2%.
The proposed method demonstrates competitive generalization capabilities to other domains, such as the Caltech CUB, Dogs and Cars datasets compared with the state of the art.
The ICNN loss is based on an inter and intra class nearest neighbors score, which helps assess the quality of embeddings obtained from the trained network.
The Proto-Triplet Loss is based on the original triplet loss with modifications needed to better work on few-shot scenarios.
The ICNN loss represents a novel loss function that evaluates the quality of features obtained based on inter/intra class, variance and class ratio from nearest neighbors.
Using the proto-triplet loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 61.32% in the 5-way 1-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
Using the proto-triplet loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 79.93% in the 5-way 5-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
Using the ICNN Loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 60.79% in the 5-way 1-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
Using the ICNN Loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 80.41% in the 5-way 5-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
The obtained accuracy performance on Mini-Imagenet represents an improvement of about 2% compared to the state of the art.
The methods are further tested on the CUB, Caltech, Stanford Dogs and Stanford Cars datasets to assess generalization capabilities, obtaining satisfactory results.

claim_records.text: The introduced flexible architecture, where class representations are conditioned for each few-shot trial based on a target image and comparisons between classes are performed by a trained network rather than relying on static metric comparison, achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Caltech-UCSD birds fine-grained classification task.

The proposed few-shot architecture replaces metric space comparison with a learned neural network, producing a softmax probability distribution rather than a true distance or similarity metric, so it is not a true metric-learning approach.
The network achieves its best performance only when it is allowed to condition each class representation based on the target, or query, image.
The network consists of four distinct stages trained fully end-to-end: a feature stage, a relational stage, a conditioning stage, and a classifier.

The feature stage uses a convolutional architecture with four convolutional blocks, each containing a 2D convolutional layer with 3×3 kernel and 32 filters, followed by batch normalization, ELU activation, and 2×2 max pooling, with a final linear layer producing an 800-dimensional image representation.
The relational stage compares images within a class in a pairwise fashion using shared parameters across all classes, producing a single vector to represent the class.
The conditioning stage uses the query image to augment the representation for each class.
The classifier stage combines information across class vectors and produces a final softmax classification based on the query image.
Relational networks for few-shot class representation are order-insensitive, allowing treatment of support set images for a single class as an unordered input set.

claim_records.text: The proposed hybrid Meta-Metric-Learner combines optimization-based and metric-based meta-learning, consisting of a task-specific metric-based learner as a base model and a meta-learner that learns and specifies the base model.
The Meta-Metric-Learner is able to handle flexible numbers of classes as well as generate more generalized metrics for classification across tasks.

Optimization-based meta-learning approaches require task-specific classifiers to be homogeneous-structured to ease parameter prediction, so they can only handle few-shot learning problems where tasks share a uniform number of classes.
Metric-based meta-learning approaches learn one task-invariant metric for all tasks, and require tasks to come from a similar domain such that a uniform metric works across tasks.

Experiments show the Meta-Metric-Learner approach obtains superior performance in both the standard k-shot N-way few-shot setting and the new realistic few-shot setting with flexible class numbers in single-source and multi-source forms.

The meta learner operating across tasks uses an optimization-based meta-model to discover good parameters and gradient descent in task-specific base learners, while the base learner exploits a metric-based model parameterized by weight prediction from the optimization-based meta-learner.
The proposed model is able to handle unbalanced classes in meta-train and meta-test sets and generate task-specific metrics leveraging weight prediction of the meta-learner given task instances.
Existing optimization-based few-shot learning approaches cannot resolve the issue of heterogeneous-structured task-specific networks arising when tasks have different numbers of labels.
The learned task-invariant metric of metric-based approaches may not generalize well if tasks diverge, and no uniform metric is suitable for all tasks from different domains or data sources.

evidence_items.claim_text: The proposed hybrid Meta-Metric-Learner combines optimization-based and metric-based meta-learning, consisting of a task-specific metric-based learner as a base model and a meta-learner that learns and specifies the base model.

evidence_items.paper_title: A Hybrid Approach with Optimization and Metric-based Meta-Learner for Few-Shot Learning
evidence_items.claim_text: The Meta-Metric-Learner is able to handle flexible numbers of classes as well as generate more generalized metrics for classification across tasks.

evidence_items.paper_title: A Hybrid Approach with Optimization and Metric-based Meta-Learner for Few-Shot Learning
evidence_items.claim_text: Optimization-based meta-learning approaches require task-specific classifiers to be homogeneous-structured to ease parameter prediction, so they can only handle few-shot learning problems where tasks share a uniform number of classes.

evidence_items.paper_title: A Hybrid Approach with Optimization and Metric-based Meta-Learner for Few-Shot Learning
evidence_items.claim_text: Metric-based meta-learning approaches learn one task-invariant metric for all tasks, and require tasks to come from a similar domain such that a uniform metric works across tasks.

evidence_items.paper_title: A Hybrid Approach with Optimization and Metric-based Meta-Learner for Few-Shot Learning
evidence_items.claim_text: Experiments show the Meta-Metric-Learner approach obtains superior performance in both the standard k-shot N-way few-shot setting and the new realistic few-shot setting with flexible class numbers in single-source and multi-source forms.

evidence_items.paper_title: A Hybrid Approach with Optimization and Metric-based Meta-Learner for Few-Shot Learning
evidence_items.claim_text: The meta learner operating across tasks uses an optimization-based meta-model to discover good parameters and gradient descent in task-specific base learners, while the base learner exploits a metric-based model parameterized by weight prediction from the optimization-based meta-learner.

evidence_items.paper_title: A Hybrid Approach with Optimization and Metric-based Meta-Learner for Few-Shot Learning
evidence_items.claim_text: The proposed model is able to handle unbalanced classes in meta-train and meta-test sets and generate task-specific metrics leveraging weight prediction of the meta-learner given task instances.

evidence_items.paper_title: A Hybrid Approach with Optimization and Metric-based Meta-Learner for Few-Shot Learning
evidence_items.claim_text: Existing optimization-based few-shot learning approaches cannot resolve the issue of heterogeneous-structured task-specific networks arising when tasks have different numbers of labels.

evidence_items.paper_title: A Hybrid Approach with Optimization and Metric-based Meta-Learner for Few-Shot Learning
evidence_items.claim_text: The learned task-invariant metric of metric-based approaches may not generalize well if tasks diverge, and no uniform metric is suitable for all tasks from different domains or data sources.

claim_records.text: The proposed adaptive metric learning approach automatically determines the best weighted combination from a set of metrics obtained from meta-training tasks for a newly seen few-shot task.

Extensive quantitative evaluations on real-world sentiment analysis and dialog intent classification datasets demonstrate that the proposed method performs favorably against state-of-the-art few shot learning algorithms in terms of predictive accuracy.

The proposed task-clustering framework for diverse few-shot learning starts with a novel task clustering algorithm based on matrix completion, followed by a few-shot learning method based on task clustering.

fact_fields.method: task-clustering framework with matrix completion-based task clustering

claim_records.text: Directly using transfer performance for task clustering requires conducting source-target transfer learning O(n^2) times, where n is the number of meta-training tasks.
For a large number of diverse tasks where n can be larger than 1,000, evaluation of the full transfer performance matrix is unacceptable because it requires over 1M entries to evaluate.
The proposed matrix completion-based task clustering algorithm deals with the huge number of transfer performance entries by randomly sampling task pairs to evaluate S_ij and S_ji scores.
The proposed matrix completion-based task clustering algorithm deals with unreliable entries and asymmetry issue by keeping only task pairs (i, j) with consistent S_ij and S_ji scores.
Few-shot learning aims to learn classifiers from few examples per class.
Deep learning-based FSL learns meta-models from a large number of meta-training tasks, which can then be used for rapid adaptation for target/meta-testing tasks that only have few training examples.

Previous FSL works mainly considered image domains such as Omniglot and ImageNet, where tasks are sampled from a single domain and thus related, leading to almost all previous works employing a common meta-model for all few-shot tasks.
In enterprise AI cloud service scenarios, submitted text classification tasks are significantly diverse, thus a common metric is insufficient to handle all these tasks.
The authors of Diverse Few-Shot Text Classification with Multiple Metrics are affiliated with AI Foundations – Learning, IBM Research, IBM T. J. Watson Research Center, Yorktown Heights, NY 10598.

claim_records.text: Deep metric learning methods for few-shot image classification classify unseen samples according to their distances to few seen samples in an embedding space learned by powerful deep neural networks, avoiding overfitting to few training images.

This review categorizes deep metric learning methods for few-shot image classification from 2018 to 2022 into three groups according to three stages of metric learning: learning feature embeddings, learning class representations, and learning distance measures.

In few-shot classification, the metric is learned on the base dataset; query images of the novel class are classified by computing their distances to novel support images with respect to the learned measure, followed by applying a distance-based classifier such as k-nearest.

fact_fields.method: supervised metric learning for few-shot classification

claim_records.text: Early few-shot metric learning methods such as Siamese Network and Matching Network classify a query sample by measuring and comparing its distance to support samples.
Class prototypes can be constructed by taking simple or weighted average of feature embeddings, or learned in an end-to-end manner to improve their representation ability.

Zhang et al. proposed a variational Bayesian framework for few-shot learning that uses the Kullback-Leibler divergence to measure the distance of samples, and can compute the confidence that a query image is assigned into each class by estimating the distribution of each class based on a neural network.

fact_fields.method: variational Bayesian framework for few-shot learning

claim_records.text: Simon et al. proposed Deep Subspace Network (DSN) to represent each class using a low-dimensional subspace constructed from support samples via singular value decomposition.

DSN classifies query samples according to the nearest subspace classifier, assigning the query to the class which has the shortest Euclidean distance between the query and its projection onto the class-specific subspace.
DSN is shown to be more robust to noises and outliers than Prototoypical Network.
Few-shot classification is defined as learning a classification rule from few (typically 1-5) labeled examples.
The biggest challenge in few-shot classification is a high risk of model overfitting to the few labeled training samples.
Meta-learning methods train a meta-learner on many different classification tasks to extract generalizable knowledge, which enables rapid learning on a new related task with few examples.
Transfer learning methods presume shared knowledge between the source and target domains, and fine-tune the model trained on abundant source data to fit few labeled target samples.

Metric learning methods learn feature embeddings and/or distance measures and classify an unseen sample based on its distance to labeled samples or class representations; samples of the same class are expected to locate close together in the embedding space and samples of different classes should be far apart.

claim_records.text: The Uncertainty-Aware Few-Shot (UAFS) framework models uncertainty of query-prototype similarity and performs uncertainty-aware optimization for few-shot image classification.

For a query sample and N prototypes in the support set, each query-prototype pair is treated as a node and a graph-based model is employed to jointly infer the similarity uncertainty for each query-prototype pair.

The similarity between a query feature and a prototype feature is modeled by a distribution (probabilistic similarity) based on graph-based similarity uncertainty estimation, rather than a scalar, to alleviate the influence of observation noises.

fact_fields.method: probabilistic similarity modeling based on graph-based similarity uncertainty estimation

claim_records.text: The network is optimized with similarity-based classification losses which exploit the estimated uncertainty.

fact_fields.method: similarity-based classification losses exploiting estimated uncertainty

claim_records.text: The proposed Uncertainty-Aware Few-Shot framework converts observed similarities to probabilistic representations and incorporates them to the loss for more effective optimization.
A graph-based model is utilized to estimate the uncertainty of query-support pairs in order to jointly consider the similarities between a query and the prototypes in a support set.
Extensive experiments show the proposed method brings significant improvements on top of a strong baseline and achieves state-of-the-art performance.

Good feature embedding is important to deliver favorable performance for similarity-based few-shot image classification, and the set of category-specific prototypes plays the role of a similarity-based classifier to identify the category of a query sample by finding the nearest prototype over the support set in the embedding space.
During training, for a query sample, the logit vector (classification probability) is obtained by feeding the similarities between the query sample and the prototypes to a SoftMax function.

fact_fields.method: SoftMax function applied to query-prototype similarities

claim_records.text: The reliability of the estimated similarity is vital to few-shot image classification performance.
Aleatoric uncertainty identifies the confidence level of the network on its output for a sample, which captures the noise inherent in the observations.

For few-shot image classification, the network has different uncertainties on the calculated similarities of different query-prototype pairs, and an observed similarity of a query-prototype pair, being a one time sampling, suffers from observation noise, where higher uncertainty means less reliable estimated similarity.
For each few-shot task during optimization, the number of experienced query-prototype pairs is limited, and the side effect of observation noises due to high uncertainty limits the optimization.

For each query-prototype pair, the proposed framework converts the observed feature similarity between the query and the prototype from a deterministic scalar to a distribution, with the variance of this distribution characterizing the uncertainty of the observed similarity.

fact_fields.method: conversion of observed feature similarity from scalar to distribution

claim_records.text: The core idea of the proposed method is to use feature-wise transformation layers for augmenting image features using affine transforms to simulate various feature distributions under different domains in the training stage.

fact_fields.method: feature-wise transformation layers with affine transforms

claim_records.text: A learning-to-learn approach is further applied to search for the hyper-parameters of the feature-wise transformation layers to capture variations of the feature distributions under different domains.
Extensive experiments and ablation studies are conducted under the domain generalization setting using five few-shot classification datasets: mini-ImageNet, CUB, Cars, Places, and Plantae.

Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed feature-wise transformation layer is applicable to various metric-based models, and provides consistent improvements on the few-shot classification performance under domain shift.

Metric-based few-shot classification methods consist of a feature encoder and a metric function: given an input task with support set and query set from novel classes, the encoder first extracts image features, and the metric function takes features of both labeled and unlabeled images as input to predict the category of query images.
Existing metric-based approaches often do not generalize well to categories from different domains, despite success recognizing novel classes sampled from the same domain as the training stage.
The key observation is that the distributions of image features extracted from tasks in unseen domains are significantly different from those in seen domains.
Unsupervised domain adaptation approaches assume that numerous unlabeled images are available in the target domain during training, which may not be realistic in many cases.
Existing domain generalization approaches aim at recognizing instances from the same category in the training stage.
During the training stage, the metric function may overfit to the feature distributions encoded only from seen domains and thus fail to generalize to unseen domains.

The proposed feature-wise transformation layers modulate feature activations with affine transformations integrated into the feature encoder, simulating various distributions of image features during training to improve the generalization ability of the metric function in the testing phase.

fact_fields.method: feature-wise transformation layers integrated into feature encoder

claim_records.text: The hyper-parameters of the feature-wise transformation layers may require meticulous hand-tuning due to the difficulty to model the complex variation of image feature distributions across various domains.

A learning-to-learn algorithm is developed to optimize the proposed feature-wise transformation layers, with the core idea to optimize the layers so that the model can work well on unseen domains after training using seen domains.
The proposed feature-wise transformation layers are method-agnostic and can be applied to various metric-based few-shot classification approaches for improving their generalization to unseen domains.

claim_records.text: Region Comparison Network (RCN) is a metric learning based method for few-shot image classification that aims to reveal how few-shot learning works in a neural network and identify specific related regions in query and support images.
Region Activation Mapping (RAM) is a visualization strategy designed to intuitively explain what RCN has learned by visualizing intermediate variables in the network.
Experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of RCN over existing baselines for few-shot image classification.
Few-shot learning aims to learn a classifier for a given set of classes using only limited labeled training samples.
Existing few-shot learning works based on metric learning include matching networks, prototypical networks, and relation networks, while gradient-based methods include MAML and MetaSGD.

fact_fields.method: metric-based and gradient-based few-shot learning models

claim_records.text: RCN's region meta learner is designed as a dynamic system to adapt to different meta tasks during the training and testing stages.

RCN directly indicates the relationship between final classification decisions and region similarities in the last layer, which is a simple and easily explained linear process compared to attention mechanisms.
RCN learns a generated weight of regions to explain which regions in a support sample are similar to regions in a query sample and which regions the model prefers to compare.

claim_records.text: On average, large-scale transfer method Big Transfer (BiT) outperforms competing approaches on the Meta-Dataset (MD) benchmark, even when trained only on ImageNet.
Meta-learning approaches struggle to compete on the Visual Task Adaptation Benchmark (VTAB) when trained and validated on Meta-Dataset (MD).
Increasing the scale of BiT does not improve performance on highly out-of-distribution MD tasks.

The VTAB+MD evaluation protocol combines the Visual Task Adaptation Benchmark (VTAB) and Meta-Dataset (MD) to enable apples-to-apples comparisons between transfer learning and meta-learning few-shot classification approaches.
BiT-L is established as state-of-the-art on the unified VTAB+MD evaluation protocol.
BiT-L does not perform better than competing approaches on Omniglot and QuickDraw, despite being significantly larger in terms of data and architecture size.

Meta-learning approaches struggle to generalize to test tasks that are significantly outside of the training task distribution, as shown by their poor performance on VTAB relative to comparable transfer learning implementations.
Transfer learning approaches for few-shot classification involve pre-training a model on an upstream dataset such as ImageNet and later fine-tuning it on downstream tasks.
Meta-learning (learning to learn) attempts to discover a learning algorithm that yields good generalization for few-shot classification problems.

claim_records.text: The Relation Network (RN) is trained end-to-end from scratch for few-shot learning.
During meta-learning, the Relation Network learns a deep distance metric to compare small numbers of images within episodes designed to simulate the few-shot setting.
Once trained, a Relation Network classifies images of new classes by computing relation scores between query images and few examples of each new class without further updating the network.
The Relation Network framework is easily extended to zero-shot learning in addition to few-shot learning.
Extensive experiments on five benchmarks demonstrate the Relation Network provides a unified and effective approach for both few-shot and zero-shot learning tasks.

claim_records.text: Existing CLIP-based few-shot classification approaches such as CoOp and Tip-Adapter only focus on high-level visual features fully aligned with textual features representing the summary of an image.
Low-level local representations (LRs) are more consistent between seen and unseen samples than high-level representations for few-shot image classification.
The proposed Meta-Feature Adaption method (MF-Adapter) combines complementary strengths of local representations and high-level semantic representations for few-shot classification.
The Meta-Feature Unit (MF-Unit) is a simple yet effective local similarity metric that measures category-consistent local context in an inductive manner.
The MF-Adapter is trained to map image features to MF-Unit to adequately generalize intra-class knowledge between unseen images and the support set.

Extensive experiments show the proposed MF-Adapter method is superior to state-of-the-art CLIP downstream few-shot classification methods, with stronger performance on a set of challenging visual classification tasks.

claim_records.text: The proposed subspace representation learning (SRL) framework represents an image using a subspace in local CNN feature space and measures similarity between two images via a weighted subspace distance (WSD).
When K images are available per class, the SRL framework develops two types of template subspaces to aggregate K-shot information: the prototypical subspace (PS) and the discriminative subspace (DS).
The SRL framework extends metric learning based techniques from vector to subspace representation.
Using subspace representation can effectively preserve the spatial structure and diversity within an image, in contrast to most previous works that adopted global vector representation.

The SRL framework demonstrates competitive or superior performance compared to previous state-of-the-art methods on the MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet, and Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 (CUB) public benchmark datasets.

claim_records.text: Local descriptor based representations can achieve richer representations than image-level based representations for few-shot learning.
Existing local descriptor based few-shot learning works still rely on a less effective instance-level symmetric metric to measure relations between query images and support classes.
An asymmetric measure is more suitable for metric-based few-shot learning, given the natural asymmetric relation between a query image and a support class.

The proposed Asymmetric Distribution Measure (ADM) network calculates a joint local and global asymmetric measure between two multivariate local distributions of queries and classes for few-shot learning.
A task-aware Contrastive Measure Strategy (CMS) is proposed to further enhance the measure function in the ADM network.
The ADM network achieves a 3.02% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task on miniImageNet.
The ADM network achieves a 1.56% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task on tieredImageNet.

claim_records.text: The RankDNN few-shot learning pipeline casts relevance ranking for image retrieval as binary ranking relation classification.
Compared to image classification, ranking relation classification is sample efficient and domain agnostic.
The core component of RankDNN is a simple MLP that takes an image triplet encoded as the difference between two vector-Kronecker products as input and outputs a binary relevance ranking order.
RankMLP can be built on top of any state-of-the-art feature extractors.
RankDNN can be flexibly fused with other post-processing methods.
During meta test, RankDNN ranks support images according to their similarity with query samples, and each query sample is assigned the class label of its nearest neighbor.
RankDNN can effectively improve the performance of its baselines based on a variety of backbones.
RankDNN outperforms previous state-of-the-art algorithms on multiple few-shot learning benchmarks including miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, Caltech-UCSD Birds, and CIFAR-FS.
Experiments on the cross-domain challenge demonstrate the superior transferability of RankDNN.

claim_records.text: The developed few-shot image classification methods employ the Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) as a metric to compute structural distance between dense image representations to determine image relevance.

fact_fields.method: Few-shot image classification methods using Earth Mover's Distance (EMD)

claim_records.text: The EMD generates optimal matching flows between structural elements that have the minimum matching cost, which is used to calculate the image distance for classification.

A cross-reference mechanism is designed to generate important weights of elements in the EMD formulation, which can effectively alleviate the adverse impact caused by cluttered background and large intra-class appearance variations.
To implement k-shot classification, a structured fully connected layer is proposed that can directly classify dense image representations with the EMD.
Based on the implicit function theorem, the EMD can be inserted as a layer into the network for end-to-end training.

fact_fields.method: Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) as a network layer

The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated on the image retrieval task in experiments.

claim_records.text: Traditional metric-based few-shot classification methods typically rely on a single distance value between the query feature and support feature, thereby overlooking the contribution of shallow features.

The proposed approach uses a multi-output embedding network that maps samples into distinct feature spaces, extracting feature vectors at different stages to enable the model to capture both global and abstract features.
Employing a self-attention mechanism improves the refinement of features at each stage, leading to even more robust representations and improved overall performance.
Assigning learnable weights to each stage significantly improved performance and results.
Comprehensive evaluations of the proposed method were conducted on the MiniImageNet and FC100 datasets, specifically in the 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot scenarios.

claim_records.text: The proposed Siamese Transformer Network (STN) uses two parallel branch networks built on the pre-trained Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture to extract global and local features respectively.
The STN implementation uses the ViT-Small network architecture, with branch networks initialized using pre-trained model parameters obtained through self-supervised learning.
STN applies the Euclidean distance measure to global features and the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence measure to local features.
STN integrates the two feature similarity metrics by first applying L2 normalization, then weighting the normalized results to obtain the final similarity score.
STN adopts a meta-learning approach to fine-tune the entire network during the training phase.
The STN framework achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines on four popular few-shot classification benchmarks in both 5-shot and 1-shot scenarios.

claim_records.text: Meta-learning has been the most common framework for few-shot learning in recent years.
Meta-learning learns the model from collections of few-shot classification tasks, which is believed to have a key advantage of making the training objective consistent with the testing objective.
Some recent works report that training for whole-classification, i.e. classification on the whole label-set, can get comparable or even better embedding than many meta-learning algorithms.
The edge between meta-learning and whole-classification lines of works has yet been underexplored, and the effectiveness of meta-learning in few-shot learning remains unclear.
The explored simple process is meta-learning over a whole-classification pre-trained model on its evaluation metric.

claim_records.text: The proposed Multi-Space Prototypical Learning (MSPL) framework for few-shot network attack detection integrates Euclidean, Cosine, Chebyshev, and Wasserstein distances through a constrained weighting scheme to enhance embedding robustness and improve pattern recognition.
MSPL leverages Polyak-averaged prototype generation to stabilize the learning process and effectively adapt to rare and zero-day attacks.
MSPL uses an episodic training paradigm to ensure balanced representation across diverse attack classes, enabling robust generalization.
Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that MSPL outperforms traditional approaches in detecting low-profile and novel attack types.

claim_records.text: Under a strictly matched iso-episode-budget protocol (250 meta-training episodes, 5 canonical seeds, 600 evaluation episodes per seed), the architecture achieves 5-shot accuracy gains consistent across all five seeds over Prototypical Networks, Relation Networks, and MAML on both CIFAR-FS and MiniImageNet.

The architecture converges in fewer training episodes than the compared baselines under the matched iso-episode-budget protocol.
The architecture generalizes better to the unseen fine-grained CUB-200-2011 birds domain with zero retraining.
The architecture is more robust to 50% occlusion and 25% spatial translation than Prototypical Networks, Relation Networks, and MAML baselines.

claim_records.text: The key issue of few-shot learning is learning to generalize.
This paper proposes a large margin principle to improve the generalization capacity of metric based methods for few-shot learning.
A unified framework is developed to learn a more discriminative metric space by augmenting the classification loss function with a large margin distance loss function for training.

Extensive experiments on graph neural networks and prototypical networks show that the proposed method can improve the performance of existing models substantially with very little computational overhead.

claim_records.text: Learning from a few examples remains a key challenge in machine learning.
The standard supervised deep learning paradigm does not offer a satisfactory solution for learning new concepts rapidly from little data.
The proposed framework learns a network that maps a small labelled support set and an unlabelled example to its label, obviating the need for fine-tuning to adapt to new class types.
The proposed algorithm improves one-shot accuracy on ImageNet from 87.6% to 93.2% compared to competing approaches.
The proposed algorithm improves one-shot accuracy on Omniglot from 88.0% to 93.8% compared to competing approaches.
The same model demonstrates usefulness on language modeling by introducing a one-shot task on the Penn Treebank.

claim_records.text: Mutual Centralized Learning (MCL) associates each local feature with a particle that can bidirectionally random walk in a discrete feature space by the affiliations.
MCL uses the features' accessibility, which measures the expected number of visits to the support features of that class in a Markov process, to estimate class probability.
MCL is related to learning a centrality on an affiliation network and can be plugged in existing methods by highlighting centralized local features.
Experiments show that MCL achieves the state-of-the-art on both miniImageNet and tieredImageNet.

claim_records.text: The proposed LaSO method combines pairs of given examples in feature space, so that the resulting synthesized feature vectors correspond to examples whose label sets are obtained through certain set operations on the label sets of the corresponding input pairs.
The LaSO method is capable of producing a sample containing the intersection, union or set-difference of labels present in two input samples.
The set operations used in LaSO generalize to labels unseen during training, enabling augmentation on examples of novel categories for multi-label few-shot classifier learning.

Experiments show promising results for the label-set manipulation capabilities of the proposed LaSO approach, both directly using classification and retrieval metrics, and in the context of performing data augmentation for multi-label few-shot learning.
The proposed LaSO method compares favorably to all the common baselines on the newly proposed benchmark for multi-label few-shot classification.

Experimental study on benchmark datasets shows the proposed DN4 achieves superiority over related state-of-the-art methods, with the largest absolute improvement of 17% over the next best method.

claim_records.text: The proposed Generative Dual Adversarial Network consists of a feature generator that generates visual features from class embeddings, a regressor that maps visual features back to corresponding class embeddings, and a discriminator that evaluates closeness between image features and class embeddings, with all components trained under combined cyclic consistency loss and dual adversarial loss.

Experimental results show the proposed model preserves higher accuracy in classifying images from seen classes while performing better than existing state-of-the-art models in classifying images from unseen classes.

claim_records.text: Existing cache-based adaptation approaches such as Tip-Adapter inherit CLIP's tendency to encode global, general-purpose representations that are not optimally discriminative for adapting the generalist to the specialist's domain in low-data regimes.

The proposed relational gated graph attention network constructs a patch graph and performs edge-aware attention to emphasize informative inter-patch interactions, producing context-enriched patch embeddings.
A learnable multi-aggregation pooling composes context-enriched patch embeddings into compact, task-discriminative representations that better align cache keys with the target few-shot classes.
The proposed graph refinement is used only during training to distil relational structure into the cache, incurring no additional inference cost beyond standard cache lookup.
Final predictions are obtained by a residual fusion of cache similarity scores with CLIP zero-shot logits.

fact_fields.method: Residual fusion of cache similarity scores with CLIP zero-shot logits

claim_records.text: Extensive evaluations on 11 benchmarks show consistent gains over state-of-the-art CLIP adapter and cache-based baselines while preserving zero-shot efficiency.

fact_fields.method: Patch-driven relational gated graph attention cache adaptation

claim_records.text: The proposed Few-shot Cosine Transformer (FS-CT) consists of two parts: a learnable prototypical embedding network to obtain categorical representations from support samples with hard cases, and a transformer encoder to effectively achieve the relational map from two different support and query samples.

Introducing Cosine Attention, a more robust and stable attention module, enhances the transformer module significantly and improves FS-CT performance from 5% to over 20% in accuracy compared to the default scaled dot-product mechanism.

fact_fields.method: FS-CT with Cosine Attention compared to FS-CT with default scaled dot-product attention

claim_records.text: The FS-CT method performs competitively in mini-ImageNet, CUB-200, and CIFAR-FS on 1-shot learning and 5-shot learning tasks across backbones and few-shot configurations.
A custom few-shot dataset for Yoga pose recognition was developed to demonstrate the potential of the FS-CT algorithm for practical application.

fact_fields.method: FS-CT algorithm evaluation on custom dataset

claim_records.text: FS-CT with cosine attention is a lightweight, simple few-shot algorithm that can be applied for a wide range of applications, such as healthcare, medical, and security surveillance.

claim_records.text: HelixFormer is a Transformer-based double-helix model designed to achieve cross-image object semantic relation mining in a bidirectional and symmetrical manner for few-shot fine-grained image classification.
HelixFormer consists of two sequential steps: 1) Relation Mining Process (RMP) across different branches, and 2) Representation Enhancement Process (REP) within each individual branch.

The designed RMP enables each HelixFormer branch to extract fine-grained object-level Cross-image Semantic Relation Maps (CSRMs) using information from the other branch, to improve cross-image interaction in semantically related local object regions.

With the aid of extracted CSRMs, the developed REP strengthens extracted features for discovered semantically-related local regions in each HelixFormer branch, boosting the model's ability to distinguish subtle fine-grained object feature differences.
Experiments conducted on five public fine-grained benchmarks show HelixFormer achieves better performance over most state-of-the-art methods under both 1-shot and 5-shot few-shot scenarios.
The official code implementation of HelixFormer is publicly available at https://github.com/JiakangYuan/HelixFormer.

claim_records.text: The proposed method shows a significant improvement in accuracy in the miniImageNet benchmark compared to other metric-based few-shot learning methods by a margin of 2%.
The proposed method demonstrates competitive generalization capabilities to other domains, such as the Caltech CUB, Dogs and Cars datasets compared with the state of the art.
The ICNN loss is based on an inter and intra class nearest neighbors score, which helps assess the quality of embeddings obtained from the trained network.
The Proto-Triplet Loss is based on the original triplet loss with modifications needed to better work on few-shot scenarios.
The ICNN loss represents a novel loss function that evaluates the quality of features obtained based on inter/intra class, variance and class ratio from nearest neighbors.
Using the proto-triplet loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 61.32% in the 5-way 1-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
Using the proto-triplet loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 79.93% in the 5-way 5-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
Using the ICNN Loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 60.79% in the 5-way 1-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
Using the ICNN Loss, the method obtains an accuracy performance of 80.41% in the 5-way 5-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
The obtained accuracy performance on Mini-Imagenet represents an improvement of about 2% compared to the state of the art.
The methods are further tested on the CUB, Caltech, Stanford Dogs and Stanford Cars datasets to assess generalization capabilities, obtaining satisfactory results.

claim_records.text: The introduced flexible architecture, where class representations are conditioned for each few-shot trial based on a target image and comparisons between classes are performed by a trained network rather than relying on static metric comparison, achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Caltech-UCSD birds fine-grained classification task.

The proposed few-shot architecture replaces metric space comparison with a learned neural network, producing a softmax probability distribution rather than a true distance or similarity metric, so it is not a true metric-learning approach.
The network achieves its best performance only when it is allowed to condition each class representation based on the target, or query, image.
The network consists of four distinct stages trained fully end-to-end: a feature stage, a relational stage, a conditioning stage, and a classifier.

The feature stage uses a convolutional architecture with four convolutional blocks, each containing a 2D convolutional layer with 3×3 kernel and 32 filters, followed by batch normalization, ELU activation, and 2×2 max pooling, with a final linear layer producing an 800-dimensional image representation.
The relational stage compares images within a class in a pairwise fashion using shared parameters across all classes, producing a single vector to represent the class.
The conditioning stage uses the query image to augment the representation for each class.
The classifier stage combines information across class vectors and produces a final softmax classification based on the query image.
Relational networks for few-shot class representation are order-insensitive, allowing treatment of support set images for a single class as an unordered input set.

claim_records.text: The proposed hybrid Meta-Metric-Learner combines optimization-based and metric-based meta-learning, consisting of a task-specific metric-based learner as a base model and a meta-learner that learns and specifies the base model.
The Meta-Metric-Learner is able to handle flexible numbers of classes as well as generate more generalized metrics for classification across tasks.

Optimization-based meta-learning approaches require task-specific classifiers to be homogeneous-structured to ease parameter prediction, so they can only handle few-shot learning problems where tasks share a uniform number of classes.
Metric-based meta-learning approaches learn one task-invariant metric for all tasks, and require tasks to come from a similar domain such that a uniform metric works across tasks.

Experiments show the Meta-Metric-Learner approach obtains superior performance in both the standard k-shot N-way few-shot setting and the new realistic few-shot setting with flexible class numbers in single-source and multi-source forms.

The meta learner operating across tasks uses an optimization-based meta-model to discover good parameters and gradient descent in task-specific base learners, while the base learner exploits a metric-based model parameterized by weight prediction from the optimization-based meta-learner.
The proposed model is able to handle unbalanced classes in meta-train and meta-test sets and generate task-specific metrics leveraging weight prediction of the meta-learner given task instances.
Existing optimization-based few-shot learning approaches cannot resolve the issue of heterogeneous-structured task-specific networks arising when tasks have different numbers of labels.
The learned task-invariant metric of metric-based approaches may not generalize well if tasks diverge, and no uniform metric is suitable for all tasks from different domains or data sources.
